clinicalPearls: Idiopathic scoliosis presenting before three years of age, an uncommon form that behaves differently from the adolescent type
Unlike the adolescent pattern, it is more frequent in boys and the curves are more often left-sided and thoracic
The curve magnitude is measured by the Cobb angle on a standing (or supine, in the non-ambulant infant) posteroanterior spinal radiograph
The rib-vertebral angle difference (Mehta angle) on the initial films helps predict which curves will resolve and which will progress
Curve behaviour during the rapid growth of early childhood is critical, as progressive early-onset curves threaten chest and lung development (thoracic insufficiency)
The higher rate of underlying neural-axis abnormality means whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging is indicated, particularly for atypical, left-sided, or progressive curves
Many curves resolve spontaneously with observation, whereas progressive curves are managed with serial derotation casting or bracing to control the deformity while allowing growth
reference.pathophysiology: Infantile idiopathic scoliosis is a three-dimensional deformity of the spine, with lateral curvature and vertebral rotation, that arises in the absence of any congenital vertebral anomaly or identifiable neuromuscular disease. Its cause is uncertain, with proposed contributions from intrauterine moulding and postnatal positioning as well as asymmetric growth of the immature spine. Because it develops during the period of most rapid spinal and pulmonary growth, progressive curves can restrict thoracic volume and impair lung development, producing thoracic insufficiency. A subset of apparently idiopathic infantile curves in fact harbour an intraspinal abnormality such as a Chiari malformation, syrinx, or tethered cord, which is why magnetic resonance imaging is important before attributing the deformity to a purely idiopathic cause.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital scoliosis from vertebral formation or segmentation anomalies
Neuromuscular scoliosis in cerebral palsy or spinal muscular atrophy
Scoliosis secondary to an intraspinal anomaly such as syrinx or tethered cord
Syndromic scoliosis, for example in neurofibromatosis or a connective-tissue disorder
Postural or compensatory curve from leg-length discrepancy
Scoliosis associated with a spinal tumour
additionalInvestigations: Standing or supine posteroanterior and lateral whole-spine radiographs with Cobb angle measurement
Rib-vertebral angle difference (Mehta angle) to assess progression risk
Whole-spine magnetic resonance imaging to exclude an intraspinal or neural-axis anomaly
Neurological examination for signs of an underlying cord abnormality
Assessment of growth, chest shape, and respiratory function in progressive curves
Evaluation for congenital or syndromic features and, where indicated, genetic assessment
redFlags: A progressive curve or a high rib-vertebral angle difference predicting progression
A left thoracic curve or other atypical pattern raising concern for an intraspinal anomaly
Neurological signs such as abnormal reflexes, weakness, or asymmetric abdominal reflexes
Impaired chest growth or respiratory compromise suggesting thoracic insufficiency
Rapid progression during periods of accelerated growth
reference.prognosis: Many infantile curves, especially those with a low rib-vertebral angle difference, resolve spontaneously with a good outcome, whereas progressive early-onset curves can become severe and threaten pulmonary development, making early identification and growth-friendly management essential.
pitfalls: Assuming an infantile curve is benign idiopathic and omitting magnetic resonance imaging of the neural axis
Failing to use the rib-vertebral angle difference to stratify progression risk
Underestimating the impact of a progressive curve on chest and lung growth
Delaying treatment of a progressive curve until the deformity is severe
Overlooking neurological signs that point to an intraspinal cause
references: Mehta MH, rib-vertebral angle difference in infantile scoliosis
management: Observe curves at low progression risk, indicated by a low rib-vertebral angle difference, with serial radiographic monitoring of the Cobb angle
Apply serial derotation (Mehta/EDF elongation-derotation-flexion) casting as first-line active treatment for progressive curves in young children, which can be curative
Use bracing to hold correction between casting phases or once casting is completed
Obtain whole-spine MRI to exclude an intraspinal anomaly such as Chiari malformation, syrinx or tethered cord before attributing a curve to idiopathic disease
Consider growth-friendly surgical instrumentation such as growing rods for severe progressive curves to preserve spinal and thoracic growth
Monitor chest shape and respiratory function to detect thoracic insufficiency in progressive early-onset curves
Refer to paediatric spinal orthopaedics and involve neurosurgery where a neural-axis abnormality is identified
